content.text: Waves are one of the most fundamental phenomena in physics. Every time you listen to music, see a rainbow, feel the warmth of the Sun, or watch ripples spread across a pond, you are experiencing waves in action. But what exactly is a wave? At its core, a wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter. This is a crucial idea: when you watch waves moving across the surface of a lake, the water itself does not travel with the wave. Instead, the water particles oscillate (move back and forth) about their rest positions, passing energy along from one particle to the next.

Understanding wave properties is essential because waves govern so much of the physical world around us. Light, sound, radio signals, earthquakes, and even the quantum behaviour of subatomic particles all involve wave phenomena. In this lesson, we will explore the fundamental properties that all waves share, learn to distinguish between the two main types of waves, and develop the mathematical tools needed to describe wave behaviour quantitatively.

A wave is a disturbance that propagates through a medium or through space, transferring energy without transferring matter. Consider a Mexican wave in a stadium: each person stands up and sits down in turn, but no person actually moves along the row of seats. The "disturbance" (the standing-up motion) travels along the crowd, but the people stay in roughly the same place. This is exactly how most waves work.
The key points to remember are:
Waves transfer energy from one place to another.
Waves are caused by oscillations (repeated back-and-forth or up-and-down movements).
A wave requires a source of energy to create the initial disturbance.

In a transverse wave, the oscillations (vibrations) of the particles are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction in which the wave travels. Imagine holding one end of a long rope and flicking your hand up and down. The wave pulse travels horizontally along the rope, but each small segment of the rope moves up and down vertically. The direction of particle vibration is at 90 degrees to the direction of wave propagation.
Water surface waves (the water moves up and down while the wave moves horizontally)
Waves on a stretched string or rope
Transverse waves have distinct peaks and troughs. The highest points are called crests and the lowest points are called troughs.

In a longitudinal wave, the oscillations of the particles are parallel to (in the same direction as) the direction in which the wave travels. A good way to visualise this is to imagine a slinky spring stretched out on a table. If you push and pull one end of the slinky back and forth along its length, you create regions where the coils are bunched together (compressions) and regions where they are spread apart (rarefactions). These compressions and rarefactions travel along the slinky, but each individual coil only moves back and forth about its rest position.
Sound waves in air, liquids, and solids
Compression waves in a slinky spring
Longitudinal waves consist of alternating compressions (regions of high pressure or high density) and rarefactions (regions of low pressure or low density).

All waves, whether transverse or longitudinal, can be described using the same set of fundamental quantities:

The amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle from its rest (equilibrium) position. For a transverse wave, this is the height of a crest or the depth of a trough measured from the undisturbed position. Amplitude is measured in metres (m). A larger amplitude means the wave carries more energy. For a sound wave, a larger amplitude means a louder sound. For a light wave, a larger amplitude means brighter light.

The wavelength is the distance between two consecutive points that are in phase with each other. For a transverse wave, this is most easily measured as the distance from one crest to the next crest, or from one trough to the next trough. For a longitudinal wave, it is the distance from one compression to the next compression, or from one rarefaction to the next rarefaction. Wavelength is measured in metres (m) and is represented by the Greek letter lambda (

The frequency is the number of complete waves (cycles) that pass a given point per second. If you stand at a fixed point and count how many wave crests pass you in one second, that number is the frequency. Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz means one complete wave per second. A wave with a frequency of 50 Hz has 50 complete cycles passing a point every second.

The period is the time taken for one complete wave (one full cycle) to pass a given point. It is also the time for one complete oscillation of any particle in the wave. Period is measured in seconds (s). The period and frequency are reciprocals of each other:
The wave speed is the distance travelled by the wave per unit time. It tells you how fast the wave pattern moves through the medium. Wave speed is measured in metres per second (m/s).

A wavefront is an imaginary line or surface that joins all points on a wave that are in the same phase of oscillation. For circular ripples spreading out from a point source on a water surface, the wavefronts are circles centred on the source. For a plane wave (such as waves far from the source, or waves in a ripple tank with a straight vibrating bar), the wavefronts are straight parallel lines.
The direction of wave travel is always perpendicular to the wavefronts. This concept is very useful when we study reflection, refraction, and diffraction in later lessons.

A ripple tank is a shallow tray of water used in laboratories to study wave behaviour. A motorised vibrating bar or a small dipper creates waves on the water surface. A lamp above the tank projects the wave pattern onto a screen below, making the wavefronts clearly visible.
Using a ripple tank, you can observe:
Straight wavefronts from a plane vibrator and circular wavefronts from a point source.
How wavelength changes when frequency is changed (higher frequency gives shorter wavelength at the same wave speed).
Reflection, refraction, and diffraction of water waves.
The relationship between wavefront spacing and wavelength.
The ripple tank is an excellent tool for visualising wave behaviour because water waves are easy to see and their behaviour mirrors the behaviour of other types of waves, including light and sound.

Many students think that because ocean waves appear to push water towards the shore, waves must transfer matter. In reality, individual water molecules move in roughly circular paths and return to approximately their starting positions after each wave passes. It is energy, not matter, that is transferred by the wave. The apparent movement of water onto a beach is caused by complex interactions near the shore, not by the wave itself carrying water forward.
Misconception 2: Amplitude is measured from crest to trough

A very common error is to measure the amplitude as the total vertical distance from crest to trough. The amplitude is actually measured from the equilibrium (rest) position to either the crest or the trough. The crest-to-trough distance is twice the amplitude.
Misconception 3: Increasing frequency increases wave speed

Students often assume that if you increase the frequency of a wave, its speed increases. In most situations, the speed of a wave is determined by the medium through which it travels, not by the frequency. If you increase the frequency while the wave speed stays the same, the wavelength must decrease (since
). The speed of sound in air at a given temperature is the same regardless of the pitch of the sound.
Misconception 4: All waves need a medium

Mechanical waves (such as sound and water waves) do need a medium to travel through. However, electromagnetic waves (such as light, radio waves, and X-rays) do not need a medium. They can travel through a vacuum. This is how energy from the Sun reaches the Earth through the vacuum of space.
Misconception 5: Wavelength is measured from any two points

Wavelength must be measured between two consecutive points that are in phase, meaning they are at exactly the same point in the wave cycle and moving in the same direction. For example, from one crest to the very next crest, or from one trough to the very next trough. Measuring from a crest to the next trough would give half a wavelength, not a full wavelength.

Sound waves have wavelengths comparable to the size of everyday obstacles and openings (wavelengths of audible sound range from about 1.7 cm to 17 m). When sound passes through a gap or around a corner, it diffracts (spreads out) significantly because the gap/obstacle size is similar to the wavelength. This allows the sound to bend around the corner and reach the listener. Visible light has a much shorter wavelength (around 400 to 700 nm), so it diffracts only a negligible amount around everyday obstacles and travels in essentially straight lines. Therefore, light does not bend noticeably around the corner, and you cannot see the person.
